Leaving out the first number is the same as using 0, the beginning of the list, and leaving out the second is the same as using the length of the list, which slices to the end (Sweigart, 2025). So spam[:2] is the first two items, spam[1:] is everything from index 1 on, and spam[:] is every item. The documentation phrases it as if i is omitted or None, use 0, and if j is omitted or None, use len(s) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The shortcuts say what the programmer means: the first n items, all but the first, a copy. They also remove two sources of error, the length that must be typed correctly and the zero that must not be forgotten. The expression spam[:] deserves a note of its own, because it is the shortest way to make a shallow copy of a list, as the documentation says: list.copy is equivalent to sequence[:] (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the executed checks, the three slices of the four animals are ['cat', 'bat'], ['bat', 'rat', 'elephant'] and the full list. The copy made by spam[:] is equal to spam but is not the same object: spam[:] == spam is True while spam[:] is spam is False. Changing the copy therefore leaves the original alone, and the checks show it. The first and the last items are available in the same way: spam[:1] is ['cat'] and spam[-1:] is ['elephant'], each a list of one item, which differs from spam[0], the item itself.

An omitted number is replaced by the end that suits the direction of the slice. With the default step of 1 the missing start is 0 and the missing end is the length. With a negative step, which the next concept explains, the missing start is the last item and the missing end is before the first, so the default is chosen by the sign of the step (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The colon itself must stay: spam[1] is an index and spam[1:] is a slice, and the two give different kinds of result.

A slice that holds one item is still a list. Code that wrote spam[:1] and expects a string will print ['cat'] with its brackets, and code that compares spam[:1] with 'cat' will never find them equal. A second trap is to assume that spam[:] is needed to loop over a list safely; it is useful only when the loop changes the list, as the concept on mutation during a loop shows.

nodes.definition: Leaving out the first number of a slice means 0 and leaving out the second means the length of the list; spam[:] is a copy of the whole list.

nodes.label: Slice step
nodes.body: The step of a slice is an optional third number after a second colon, and it sets the distance between the items that are taken. The slice s[i:j:k] is the sequence of items with index x = i + n*k, stopping when j is reached but never including j (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The step cannot be zero. A step of 1 is the default, a step of 2 takes every second item, and a negative step takes the items from the end towards the front. This concept is not in the chapter; it comes from the documentation of the sequence types.

paras.text: The step of a slice is an optional third number after a second colon, and it sets the distance between the items that are taken. The slice s[i:j:k] is the sequence of items with index x = i + n*k, stopping when j is reached but never including j (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The step cannot be zero. A step of 1 is the default, a step of 2 takes every second item, and a negative step takes the items from the end towards the front. This concept is not in the chapter; it comes from the documentation of the sequence types.

The step completes the notation and gives two idioms that appear in real programs. The slice s[::2] takes the items at even positions, and s[1::2] those at odd positions, which separates the two values of an interleaved list. The slice s[::-1] is the shortest way to make a reversed copy of a list. The chapter teaches the reverse() method, which reverses a list in place; the slice step makes a new, reversed list and leaves the original alone.

In the executed checks list(range(10))[::3] is [0, 3, 6, 9], list(range(10))[1::2] is [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], and list(range(5))[::-1] is [4, 3, 2, 1, 0]. The reversed copy is a new list: reversing the slice does not touch the original list. A step of 0 is refused with a ValueError whose message is slice step cannot be zero. The tutorial's looping techniques also reverse a sequence for a loop, and use the reversed function for it, which does not build a copy (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

With a positive step the start defaults to the first item and the end to the length; with a negative step the start defaults to the last item and the end to before the first item. When the step is not 1, an assignment to the slice needs a list of exactly the same length as the slice, but reading is always allowed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Slices with a step still return a new list. For a list of ten items [::3] touches indexes 0, 3, 6 and 9, which are four items, so the length of the result is the ceiling of 10 divided by 3.

The step is a part of Python's slice notation that the chapter does not cover. It is in the course because a student who reads other people's code will meet [::-1] and [::2] long before meeting the reverse() method in a program. The idiom [::-1] works on strings and tuples as well, since they are sequences too, but not on a set or a dictionary.

nodes.definition: A slice can carry a third number, the step: s[i:j:k] takes every kth item, and a negative step walks backwards, so s[::-1] is a reversed copy.

nodes.label: Changing a list
nodes.body: Lists can be changed after they are made, and this branch explains every way the chapter changes them: replacing an item by assignment to its index, adding items with append, insert and extend, removing them with del, remove and pop, and combining lists with the operators + and *. A list is a mutable data type, which means that you can add, remove or change its values (Sweigart, 2025). All of these operations change the list in place or build a new list, and the difference between the two is the thread that runs through the branch.

paras.text: Lists can be changed after they are made, and this branch explains every way the chapter changes them: replacing an item by assignment to its index, adding items with append, insert and extend, removing them with del, remove and pop, and combining lists with the operators + and *. A list is a mutable data type, which means that you can add, remove or change its values (Sweigart, 2025). All of these operations change the list in place or build a new list, and the difference between the two is the thread that runs through the branch.

A program that handles a collection nearly always changes it: it collects names as a user types them, removes the ones that have been dealt with, puts a new one in the middle. A programmer who knows the full set of operations and which of them change the list, which return a new list and which return the removed item can write each of these steps in one line, and can read at a glance what a line of someone else's program does to its data.

The operations of this branch are used in nearly every program of the course. The cat names program of the chapter grows a list one name at a time. The Magic 8 Ball program of a later concept is easy to extend because its answers are items of a list that can be added or removed without changing the other lines of the program. The text and file chapters build lists of lines with append and clean them with remove and pop.

The branch has four groups. Replacing explains assignment to an index. Adding explains append, insert and extend. Removing explains the del statement and the methods remove and pop. Combining explains the operators + and * and the augmented assignment operators, which for lists are an in-place variant of the same operations. Within the groups, each concept states what the operation returns, because that is the fact that most often decides whether a line is right.

nodes.label: Replacing items
nodes.body: Replacing an item is the simplest change to a list: the item at a given position is thrown away and another value takes its place. The group has one concept, assignment to an index, which uses the notation that reads an item on the left of an assignment statement. The chapter shows it with assignment to an index of the same list of animals (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Replacing an item is the simplest change to a list: the item at a given position is thrown away and another value takes its place. The group has one concept, assignment to an index, which uses the notation that reads an item on the left of an assignment statement. The chapter shows it with assignment to an index of the same list of animals (Sweigart, 2025).

Replacement changes the list and not the variable. The name still refers to the same list afterwards, and every other name that refers to the same list sees the new item. That is the first place in the chapter where the difference between changing a value and rebinding a name matters, and it is the reason the chapter on references later returns to it.

The concept explains the assignment spam[1] = 'aardvark', its use with negative indexes, the case where the new value is another item of the same list and the IndexError that an index outside the list causes.

nodes.label: Item assignment
nodes.body: Item assignment puts a variable name on the left of an assignment statement normally, as in spam = 42, but a list index can stand there instead: the assignment changes the value at that index (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant'], the statement spam[1] = 'aardvark' means that the value at index 1 in the list spam is assigned the string 'aardvark', and the list becomes ['cat', 'aardvark', 'rat', 'elephant']. Negative indexes work too, so spam[-1] = 12345 replaces the last item. The documentation lists the operation as s[i] = x, item i of s is replaced by x (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Item assignment puts a variable name on the left of an assignment statement normally, as in spam = 42, but a list index can stand there instead: the assignment changes the value at that index (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant'], the statement spam[1] = 'aardvark' means that the value at index 1 in the list spam is assigned the string 'aardvark', and the list becomes ['cat', 'aardvark', 'rat', 'elephant']. Negative indexes work too, so spam[-1] = 12345 replaces the last item. The documentation lists the operation as s[i] = x, item i of s is replaced by x (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

This is the operation that makes the list mutable. A string has no such statement, and the chapter shows later that name[7] = 'the' on a string raises a TypeError. For a list the assignment changes the stored value, so a program can keep one list for the whole of its life and update it as it goes: a score in a game, the status of a task, a counter in each column of the Matrix screensaver, where columns[i] -= 1 counts a column down.

The chapter's own sequence of assignments shows the possible cases. After spam[1] = 'aardvark' the list is ['cat', 'aardvark', 'rat', 'elephant']; after spam[2] = spam[1] it is ['cat', 'aardvark', 'aardvark', 'elephant'], because the new value is read from the list before it is stored; after spam[-1] = 12345 the last item is the integer 12345, which shows that the new value need not have the same type as the old (Sweigart, 2025). The length is 4 before and after each step.

Python evaluates the right-hand side first, then the index, and then stores a reference to the new value in the place the index names. The old value is not touched; the list simply no longer refers to it. The place must exist: an assignment to spam[4] on a list of four items raises an IndexError whose message is list assignment index out of range. Assignment never makes a list longer, which is what append and insert are for.

Changing a list through an index changes it for every name that refers to it. If eggs = spam was written earlier, eggs[1] = 'Hello!' also changes spam, because there is only one list, and the references concept shows this in detail. Assigning to a loop variable is not the same thing: in for item in spam, writing item = 0 rebinds the name item and leaves the list alone, so a loop that must change the items has to assign to spam[i] by index.

nodes.definition: Assigning to an index replaces the item at that position, in place; the length of the list does not change.

nodes.label: Adding items
nodes.body: Adding items makes a list longer. Three methods do it: append puts one item at the end, insert puts one item at any position, and extend puts all the items of another list at the end. They are methods of the list type, which is why they can be called only on lists. The chapter teaches append and insert (Sweigart, 2025), and the documentation adds extend (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Adding items makes a list longer. Three methods do it: append puts one item at the end, insert puts one item at any position, and extend puts all the items of another list at the end. They are methods of the list type, which is why they can be called only on lists. The chapter teaches append and insert (Sweigart, 2025), and the documentation adds extend (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A program seldom knows its data in advance, and growth is the usual way a list is filled. Choosing the method that matches the intention keeps the code short and the list correct: an item that belongs at the end, an item that belongs at a chosen position, and a whole batch of items are three different intentions with three different methods.
The first concept explains append and the None that it returns, the second explains insert and its index, and the third explains extend and why it differs from append when the argument is a list.

nodes.label: Append
nodes.body: The append method adds its argument to the end of the list. With spam holding ['cat', 'dog', 'bat'], the call spam.append('moose') makes the list ['cat', 'dog', 'bat', 'moose'] (Sweigart, 2025). The documentation describes it as adding an item to the end of the list, similar to a[len(a):] = [x] (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is a method, so it is called on a list value with a dot, and the value before the dot is the list that changes.

paras.text: The append method adds its argument to the end of the list. With spam holding ['cat', 'dog', 'bat'], the call spam.append('moose') makes the list ['cat', 'dog', 'bat', 'moose'] (Sweigart, 2025). The documentation describes it as adding an item to the end of the list, similar to a[len(a):] = [x] (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is a method, so it is called on a list value with a dot, and the value before the dot is the list that changes.

Appending is the usual way to build a list one item at a time, and it is the operation that the chapter's cat names program should use. That program writes cat_names = cat_names + [name], which builds a whole new list on every pass and assigns it to the same variable (Sweigart, 2025); cat_names.append(name) does the same job by changing the list in place. The chapter's own remark is the important rule: the return value of append is None, so the call must not be assigned to the variable.

In the executed checks, spam.append('moose') leaves ['cat', 'dog', 'bat', 'moose'] and raises no error. The statement spam = spam.append('moose') is the bug the chapter warns about: the list is changed, and then the name spam is rebound to the result of the call, which is None. After it, len(spam) raises a TypeError with the message object of type 'NoneType' has no len(). Calling append on a string raises an AttributeError, because append belongs to lists only: 'str' object has no attribute 'append' (Sweigart, 2025).

The method adds exactly one item, whatever it is. When the argument is a list, that list becomes one new item and the result is a nested list: appending [1, 2] to [0] gives [0, [1, 2]] and not [0, 1, 2]. Python grows the list with spare room, so appending to the end is fast however long the list is, which makes the list a good stack: the tutorial adds items with append and takes the last one back with pop (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The return value is None for every method that changes a list in place; the documentation calls this a design principle for all mutable data structures in Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Its reason is that a programmer who writes y = y + [10] and y.append(10) is doing two different things, one making a new object and one changing the old, and the language makes the second easy to tell apart. When a line using append prints None, look for an assignment around the call.

nodes.definition: The append method adds its argument as one item to the end of the list, changes the list in place and returns None.

nodes.label: Insert
nodes.body: The insert method can insert a value at any index in the list. Its first argument is the index of the new value and its second argument is the new value (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'dog', 'bat'], spam.insert(1, 'chicken') makes the list ['cat', 'chicken', 'dog', 'bat']. The documentation says that the index is the position before which the item is inserted, so a.insert(0, x) inserts at the front of the list and a.insert(len(a), x) is equivalent to a.append(x) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The insert method can insert a value at any index in the list. Its first argument is the index of the new value and its second argument is the new value (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'dog', 'bat'], spam.insert(1, 'chicken') makes the list ['cat', 'chicken', 'dog', 'bat']. The documentation says that the index is the position before which the item is inserted, so a.insert(0, x) inserts at the front of the list and a.insert(len(a), x) is equivalent to a.append(x) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Where append can only grow a list at its end, insert keeps a list in an order the programmer decides: a new task before the others, a new name in its alphabetical place. It is the method to remember when an item has to go to the front. It has a price that append does not have, which the documentation states plainly: inserts and pops from the beginning of a list are slow, because all of the other elements have to be shifted by one (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the executed checks, inserting 'chicken' at index 1 gives ['cat', 'chicken', 'dog', 'bat']; inserting at index 0 puts the new item first; and inserting at an index larger than the length puts the item at the end, so insert(100, 'x') on a list of three items gives the same result as append('x'). Like append, insert returns None, so spam = spam.insert(1, 'chicken') would leave spam holding None. The chapter shows the AttributeError for a number: bacon = 42 followed by bacon.insert(1, 'world') fails with 'int' object has no attribute 'insert' (Sweigart, 2025).

Python makes room by moving every item from the index to the end one place to the right, writes the new reference into the gap, and increases the length by one. That movement is why the cost grows with the number of items after the index. A negative index counts from the end, as everywhere, and an index beyond either end is treated as the end it is nearest to, so insert never raises an IndexError.

A list that is used as a queue, with items added at one end and taken from the other, is better served by collections.deque than by insert(0, x), as the tutorial says (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The second trap is the argument order: insert takes the index first and the value second, the opposite of the order in which the result is read, and swapping them silently inserts the wrong thing at the wrong place when both are integers.

nodes.definition: The insert method puts an item at a chosen index and moves the items from that index on one place along; like append it changes the list and returns None.

nodes.label: Extend
nodes.body: The extend method adds all the items of another sequence to the end of a list, one by one. The documentation describes it as extending the list by appending all the items from the iterable, similar to a[len(a):] = iterable (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This method is not in the chapter, which concatenates lists with the plus operator and the augmented assignment +=. It is in the course because += on a list is a call to extend, and a reader who knows that understands why += changes the list in place.

paras.text: The extend method adds all the items of another sequence to the end of a list, one by one. The documentation describes it as extending the list by appending all the items from the iterable, similar to a[len(a):] = iterable (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This method is not in the chapter, which concatenates lists with the plus operator and the augmented assignment +=. It is in the course because += on a list is a call to extend, and a reader who knows that understands why += changes the list in place.

It answers the question of how to add a batch. A loop of append calls does the same, and so does spam = spam + other, but extend states the intention in one call and, unlike the plus operator, does not build a second list. It also accepts any iterable, so a list can be extended by the characters of a string, by a range or by the keys of a dictionary, while the plus operator needs two lists.

In the executed checks, [1, 2, 3] extended by ['A', 'B'] is [1, 2, 3, 'A', 'B'], and the same list extended by 'ab' is [1, 2, 3, 'a', 'b'], because a string is an iterable of characters. The difference from append is visible in the lengths: appending the list ['A', 'B'] to [1, 2, 3] gives a list of length 4 whose last item is a list, while extending gives length 5. The call returns None.

Python walks over the argument and appends each item it produces, so the argument is read once, from start to end. If the argument is the list itself, as in spam.extend(spam), the call is still defined: it doubles the list. The argument must be iterable; extending by a number raises a TypeError with the message 'int' object is not iterable.

The method belongs to the standard list type from the first Python 3 releases, and the course adds it because lists built from many pieces are common in the later chapters, for instance when the rows of several files are collected into one list. The tutorial lists extend beside append and insert as the three ways to add to a list (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: The extend method adds every item of an iterable to the end of the list, one by one, in place; unlike append it does not nest a list argument.

nodes.label: Removing items
nodes.body: Removing items makes a list shorter. The chapter gives two ways, the del statement, which takes an index, and the remove method, which takes a value. The documentation adds a third, the pop method, which takes an index and also hands the removed item back.

paras.text: Removing items makes a list shorter. The chapter gives two ways, the del statement, which takes an index, and the remove method, which takes a value. The documentation adds a third, the pop method, which takes an index and also hands the removed item back.

The three differ in what the programmer knows and what the program needs afterwards. The del statement is for the case where the position is known, the remove method for the case where the value is known, and pop for the case where the removed item will be used. The chapter states the first two as a rule: del is useful when you know the index of the value you want to remove, while remove is useful when you know the value itself (Sweigart, 2025).
The first concept explains del and the shift of the later items, the second explains remove and the ValueError, the third explains pop and its use as a stack.

nodes.label: Del statement
nodes.body: The del statement deletes the values at an index in a list. All the values after the deleted value move up one index (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant'], del spam[2] leaves ['cat', 'bat', 'elephant'], and a second del spam[2] leaves ['cat', 'bat']. The statement also deletes slices, so del a[2:4] removes two items and del a[:] empties the list, as the tutorial shows (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The del statement deletes the values at an index in a list. All the values after the deleted value move up one index (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant'], del spam[2] leaves ['cat', 'bat', 'elephant'], and a second del spam[2] leaves ['cat', 'bat']. The statement also deletes slices, so del a[2:4] removes two items and del a[:] empties the list, as the tutorial shows (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The del statement is the way to remove by position, and it works on a range of positions at once, which the methods cannot do. It also does something the other removals do not: used on a simple variable it deletes the name, as if it were an unassignment statement. The chapter notes that in practice you almost never need to delete simple variables, but the statement is most useful for deleting values from lists (Sweigart, 2025).

In the executed checks, the chapter's two deletions leave ['cat', 'bat', 'elephant'] and then ['cat', 'bat'], so the same index names a different item each time. On the tutorial's list a = [-1, 1, 66.25, 333, 333, 1234.5], del a[0] leaves [1, 66.25, 333, 333, 1234.5], then del a[2:4] leaves [1, 66.25, 1234.5], and del a[:] leaves []. After del on a plain variable the name no longer exists, and using it raises a NameError whose message is name 'spam' is not defined (Sweigart, 2025).

The statement is not a function and returns nothing. Deleting a list item removes the reference to it, moves the later references forward and reduces the length by one. The language reference says that deletion of a slicing is in general equivalent to assignment of an empty slice of the right type (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An index outside the list raises an IndexError: del spam[10] on a list of four items fails with the message list assignment index out of range.

Because the later items move up, deleting inside a loop over the same list skips items, which the concept on mutation during a loop shows. Deleting several items by index from the front forward is a classic mistake for the same reason: after del spam[1], the item that was at index 2 is now at index 1. Delete from the back forward, or build a new list of the items to keep.

nodes.definition: The del statement deletes the item at an index, or a slice, or a whole variable; the items after a deleted item move up one place.

nodes.label: Remove
nodes.body: The remove method accepts a value to remove from the list on which it is called (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant'], spam.remove('bat') leaves ['cat', 'rat', 'elephant']. If the value appears more than once, the method removes only the first instance, so removing 'cat' from ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'cat', 'hat', 'cat'] leaves ['bat', 'rat', 'cat', 'hat', 'cat']. The documentation phrases it as removing the first item from the list whose value is equal to value (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The remove method accepts a value to remove from the list on which it is called (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant'], spam.remove('bat') leaves ['cat', 'rat', 'elephant']. If the value appears more than once, the method removes only the first instance, so removing 'cat' from ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'cat', 'hat', 'cat'] leaves ['bat', 'rat', 'cat', 'hat', 'cat']. The documentation phrases it as removing the first item from the list whose value is equal to value (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The method removes by what an item is and not by where it is, which is how people think about a collection: take Pooka off the list, not the item at index 1. Together with the del statement it completes the pair the chapter describes, since del suits the case where the position is known and remove the case where the value is known (Sweigart, 2025). The call returns None and the list changes in place.

Asking to remove a value that is not there raises a ValueError. For spam holding the four animals, spam.remove('chicken') fails under Python 3.14 with ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list, the message the chapter prints as well (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed checks, removing 'cat' once from the six-item list leaves five items and still holds two cats, and removing an item changes the list but not the other names for the item, since the item itself is not destroyed while something refers to it.

Python compares the argument with the items from the front using ==, stops at the first equal one, deletes it and closes the gap. Equal means equal, not identical: 1 and 1.0 are equal, so remove(1) removes a 1.0 if it comes first. The cost grows with the position of the match, and a failed search walks the whole list before it raises the error.

Two traps follow from the rules. The error for a missing value can be avoided with a membership test, if 'chicken' in spam, before the call, or caught with try and except. And removing every copy of a value needs a loop, but not a for loop over the same list, which would skip items; the safe way is to build a new list without the value, as the concept on list comprehensions shows, or to repeat while the value is in the list.

nodes.definition: The remove method deletes the first item equal to its argument and raises a ValueError when there is none; it returns None.

nodes.label: Pop
nodes.body: The pop method removes an item from a list and gives it back. The documentation says it removes the item at the given position and returns it, and that with no index a.pop() removes and returns the last item (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It raises an IndexError if the list is empty or the index is outside the list range. This method is not in the chapter, which teaches del and remove; it is in the course because it is the one removal that returns what it removed.

paras.text: The pop method removes an item from a list and gives it back. The documentation says it removes the item at the given position and returns it, and that with no index a.pop() removes and returns the last item (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It raises an IndexError if the list is empty or the index is outside the list range. This method is not in the chapter, which teaches del and remove; it is in the course because it is the one removal that returns what it removed.

A removal that returns its item is what a stack needs, and the stack is the most useful structure to build from a list. The tutorial shows the rule: to add an item to the top of the stack use append, and to retrieve an item from the top use pop without an explicit index, so that the last element added is the first retrieved (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is also what a program wants when it processes a list of tasks one at a time and must not process a task twice.

In the executed checks, popping the list [3, 4, 5] returns 5 and leaves [3, 4]; pop(0) on the same list returns 3 and leaves [4, 5]. On the empty list the call fails with IndexError: pop from empty list. The tutorial's stack example appends 6 and 7 to [3, 4, 5] and then pops 7, 6 and 5 in that order, leaving [3, 4], which is a last-in, first-out order (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Python reads the item at the index, removes it as del would, and returns the item. Popping from the end is fast because nothing has to move; popping from the front moves every other item, which is why the tutorial recommends collections.deque for a queue (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An index that is out of range raises an IndexError whose message is pop index out of range.

A pop inside a loop over the same list has the same problem as a deletion there, and an unchecked pop() on an empty list ends a program. Test the list first: because an empty list counts as false, if spam: spam.pop() is the idiom, and it is in line with the style guide's advice to use the fact that empty sequences are false (van Rossum, Warsaw and Coghlan, 2001).

nodes.definition: The pop method removes the item at an index, by default the last one, and returns it; it raises an IndexError on an empty list.

nodes.label: Combining lists
nodes.body: Combining lists means making a longer list from shorter ones. The operators of the group are the plus operator, which joins two lists, the star operator, which repeats a list, and the augmented assignment operators, which do the same job and store the result in the same name.

paras.text: Combining lists means making a longer list from shorter ones. The operators of the group are the plus operator, which joins two lists, the star operator, which repeats a list, and the augmented assignment operators, which do the same job and store the result in the same name.

The operators are the same ones that work on numbers and strings, and the chapter uses that familiarity: lists can be concatenated and replicated with the + and * operators, just like strings (Sweigart, 2025). They differ from the methods of the previous groups in one respect that decides how they are used: the plus and star operators return a new list and leave their operands alone, while the augmented forms change a list in place.
The first concept explains the plus operator, the second the star operator, and the third the augmented assignment operators, in which the difference between a new list and a changed one is clearest.

nodes.label: List concatenation
nodes.body: List concatenation joins two lists end to end with the plus operator. The expression [1, 2, 3] + ['A', 'B', 'C'] evaluates to [1, 2, 3, 'A', 'B', 'C']. The + operator combines two lists to create a new list value (Sweigart, 2025). The documentation defines s + t as the concatenation of s and t and lists it among the operations that most sequence types support (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: List concatenation joins two lists end to end with the plus operator. The expression [1, 2, 3] + ['A', 'B', 'C'] evaluates to [1, 2, 3, 'A', 'B', 'C']. The + operator combines two lists to create a new list value (Sweigart, 2025). The documentation defines s + t as the concatenation of s and t and lists it among the operations that most sequence types support (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Concatenation is the easiest way to build a list from parts, and it is exact about what it does not do: both original lists are unchanged. That is useful when the originals are needed later, and wasteful when they are not, because every + builds a new list and copies the items of both. The chapter's cat names program writes cat_names = cat_names + [name], a concatenation that rebinds the variable on each pass; the documentation observes that building up a sequence by repeated concatenation has a quadratic runtime cost in the total length (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the executed checks, the sum of the two lists has six items, and after spam = [1, 2, 3] and spam = spam + ['A', 'B', 'C'] the variable holds [1, 2, 3, 'A', 'B', 'C'], the assignment being the step that makes the result stick. The result is a different object from both operands: a + b is a is False. Concatenating a list with a tuple fails with a TypeError, because the two kinds do not mix: can only concatenate list (not 'tuple') to list. To add a single item, the item must be wrapped in a list, as in spam + ['A'].

Python allocates a new list of the combined length and copies the references of the first operand and then of the second into it. The items themselves are not copied, so a nested list appears in both the old and the new list, a point the concept on shallow copies returns to. The operator is left-associative, so a + b + c builds one intermediate list, a + b, before the final result.

A plus sign between a list and a non-list is a type error and not a conversion, so spam + 'A' raises a TypeError, and spam + ['A'] is the right form. When many pieces are joined in a loop, a list that is changed in place with append or extend is faster than one that is rebuilt with the plus operator at every pass. And a concatenation whose result is not assigned to anything has no effect on any name; the expression is computed and thrown away.

nodes.definition: The + operator joins two lists into a new list and leaves both operands unchanged; both operands must be lists.

nodes.label: List replication
nodes.body: List replication repeats a list a given number of times with the star operator. The expression ['X', 'Y', 'Z'] * 3 evaluates to ['X', 'Y', 'Z', 'X', 'Y', 'Z', 'X', 'Y', 'Z']. The * operator combines a list and an integer value to replicate the list (Sweigart, 2025). The documentation says s * n is equivalent to adding s to itself n times, and that values of n less than 0 are treated as 0, which yields an empty sequence (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: List replication repeats a list a given number of times with the star operator. The expression ['X', 'Y', 'Z'] * 3 evaluates to ['X', 'Y', 'Z', 'X', 'Y', 'Z', 'X', 'Y', 'Z']. The * operator combines a list and an integer value to replicate the list (Sweigart, 2025). The documentation says s * n is equivalent to adding s to itself n times, and that values of n less than 0 are treated as 0, which yields an empty sequence (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The star operator is the shortest way to make a list of a fixed size filled with one starting value. The chapter's Matrix screensaver starts with columns = [0] * WIDTH, a list of seventy zeros, one counter for each column of output (Sweigart, 2025). The same idea gives a row of blanks, a list of zero scores or a template that a program later fills in by assigning to indexes.

In the executed checks, [0] * 3 is [0, 0, 0], ['X', 'Y', 'Z'] * 3 has nine items, [0] * 0 is [], and [0] * -2 is [], since a negative count is treated as zero. Writing the integer first, 3 * [0], gives the same result. A float count such as [0] * 2.0 raises a TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float'. Replication works on strings and tuples as well, so 'ab' * 2 is 'abab'.

Python builds a new list of the count times the length and fills it with references to the items of the original, in order. The items are not copied, they are referenced several times, as the documentation puts it (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For numbers and strings this makes no difference, because they cannot be changed. For an item that is itself a list it makes all the difference, because the repeated references all lead to one list.

The sentence just quoted is the root of a well-known bug: [[0] * 3] * 4 is a list of four references to one inner list of three zeros, and assigning to one of its places shows up in all four rows. The concept on replication and aliasing shows the bug in the interpreter and the repair with a list comprehension. Use the star operator to repeat immutable items and a comprehension to build independent lists.

nodes.definition: The * operator repeats a list the given number of times in a new list; the repeated items are the same objects, not copies.

nodes.label: Augmented assignment
nodes.body: An augmented assignment operator combines a binary operator with an assignment. When assigning a value to a variable, the variable itself is frequently used, as in spam = spam + 1, and as a shortcut the operator += does the same thing (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter's Table 6-1 lists the operators for the arithmetic signs + - * / and %, each equal to the longhand statement. The += operator can also do string and list concatenation, and the *= operator can do string and list replication (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: An augmented assignment operator combines a binary operator with an assignment. When assigning a value to a variable, the variable itself is frequently used, as in spam = spam + 1, and as a shortcut the operator += does the same thing (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter's Table 6-1 lists the operators for the arithmetic signs + - * / and %, each equal to the longhand statement. The += operator can also do string and list concatenation, and the *= operator can do string and list replication (Sweigart, 2025).

Beyond saving keystrokes, the augmented operators tell the reader that the new value is derived from the old one. For lists they carry a difference that the longhand form lacks, and the language reference states it carefully: x += 1 can be rewritten as x = x + 1 to achieve a similar, but not exactly equal effect, because in the augmented version x is evaluated only once and, when possible, the operation is performed in place, so the old object is modified instead of a new one being created (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

For a list, spam += ['A'] extends the list in place. In the executed checks, after b = a for a = [1] and a += [2], both a and b are [1, 2], because there is one list; but after b = a and a = a + [2], a is [1, 2] and b is still [1], because the plus operator built a new list and rebound a. The star form works the same way: bacon = ['Zophie'] followed by bacon *= 3 gives ['Zophie', 'Zophie', 'Zophie'] (Sweigart, 2025). For a tuple the same operator creates a new tuple, since a tuple cannot be changed.

For a mutable type Python calls the method that changes the object in place, which for lists is the one behind extend, and then assigns the returned object, the same list, back to the target. For an immutable type there is no in-place method, so Python falls back on the ordinary operator and binds the name to the new object. This is why the same operator can change a list but not a tuple, a string or an integer, and why the FAQ calls the augmented assignment operators the one class of operations where the same operation sometimes behaves differently on different types (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The in-place behaviour surprises programmers who pass a list to a function and use += on it there, because the caller's list changes too, whereas with the plus operator it would not. When a program must not change its argument, copy first or use the longhand form. The right-hand side of += on a list must be iterable, so spam += 'ab' appends two characters and spam += 5 raises a TypeError.

nodes.definition: An augmented assignment such as += or *= combines an operator with an assignment; for a list it changes the list in place.

nodes.label: Searching and ordering
nodes.body: Once a list holds many items, a program needs to ask questions of it and to arrange it: is this value in the list, where is it, which item comes first. This branch explains the methods that answer such questions and put the items in order. It starts with what a method is, then covers the in and not in operators, the index method and the short-circuiting of the Boolean operators that lets a program test before it reads, and it ends with sorting and reversing (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Once a list holds many items, a program needs to ask questions of it and to arrange it: is this value in the list, where is it, which item comes first. This branch explains the methods that answer such questions and put the items in order. It starts with what a method is, then covers the in and not in operators, the index method and the short-circuiting of the Boolean operators that lets a program test before it reads, and it ends with sorting and reversing (Sweigart, 2025).

Searching and ordering are the two services that people ask of a collection more than any other. A phone book is useful because a name can be found and because the names are in order. The same two services make a list of results, names or readings usable by a program, and the chapter's rule about which of these operations change the list and which give a new value is a rule the rest of the course relies on.

The operators and methods of this branch appear in programs that check input against a list of allowed words, in programs that look up the position of a record, and in programs that sort the lines of a report. The sorted lists of file names that the file chapters return, and the ordered rows that the spreadsheet chapters write, come from the same operations (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The branch has three groups. The first explains what a method is and why a method belongs to one data type. The second, searching, explains in, not in, index and the short-circuit rule. The third, ordering, explains sort with its key and reverse arguments, reverse, and the built-in function sorted that returns a new list and leaves the original alone.

nodes.label: Calling methods
nodes.body: A method is the same thing as a function, except that it is called on a value (Sweigart, 2025). This group has one concept, the list method, which is the form in which almost every operation of this branch and of the previous one is written: the value, a period, the name and the arguments.

paras.text: A method is the same thing as a function, except that it is called on a value (Sweigart, 2025). This group has one concept, the list method, which is the form in which almost every operation of this branch and of the previous one is written: the value, a period, the name and the arguments.

Methods are how the data types of Python carry their own operations. A learner who understands that spam.index('hello') is a function that is tied to the list in spam can read every later method, of strings, of dictionaries and of files, in the same way.
The concept shows the call, explains the idea of a function that is always associated with a value, and shows the error that follows when a method is called on a value of the wrong type.

nodes.label: Method
nodes.body: A method is the same thing as a function, except it is called on a value. A list stored in spam is searched with the index method by writing spam.index('hello'): the method part comes after the value, separated by a period (Sweigart, 2025). Each data type has its own set of methods, and the list type has several for finding, adding, removing and otherwise manipulating the values in a list. The chapter asks the reader to think of a method as a function that is always associated with a value; the function would hypothetically be index(spam, 'hello'), but since index is a list method and not a function in general, it is written after the value.

paras.text: A method is the same thing as a function, except it is called on a value. A list stored in spam is searched with the index method by writing spam.index('hello'): the method part comes after the value, separated by a period (Sweigart, 2025). Each data type has its own set of methods, and the list type has several for finding, adding, removing and otherwise manipulating the values in a list. The chapter asks the reader to think of a method as a function that is always associated with a value; the function would hypothetically be index(spam, 'hello'), but since index is a list method and not a function in general, it is written after the value.

The notation tells the reader at a glance which value an operation works on, and it keeps the operations of a type together. A programmer who wants to know what can be done with a list asks the list: the documentation lists the methods of the mutable sequence types in one place, and the built-in function dir shows the names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Because the method belongs to the value, the same word can mean different things for different types, as index does for a list and for a string.

In the executed examples ['hello', 'hi'].index('hello') is 0. Methods belong to a single data type: the methods append and insert are list methods and can be called on list values only, not on strings or integers. The expression 'hello'.append('world') raises an AttributeError whose message is 'str' object has no attribute 'append', and the integer 42 raises the message 'int' object has no attribute 'insert' when insert is called on it (Sweigart, 2025).

When Python meets spam.index('hello') it evaluates spam, looks for the name index in the type of that value, and calls what it finds with the value as the first argument and the other arguments after it. This is why the hypothetical function index(spam, 'hello') of the chapter is a faithful picture: the method call and the function call do the same work, and the type of the value decides which function is found. If the type has no such name, the lookup fails with an AttributeError.

Two slips belong here. The first is to call a list method on something that is not a list, usually because an earlier step returned a string or None; the AttributeError names the type, and the type in the message is the first clue. The second is to leave out the parentheses: spam.append is a bound method object and not a call, and nothing is appended. The chapter on functions explains the parentheses; here it is enough to check that every method call has them.

nodes.definition: A method is a function that is called on a value, written value.name(arguments); each data type has its own methods, and calling a list method on a string raises an AttributeError.

nodes.label: Searching a list
nodes.body: Searching a list means asking where a value is or whether it is there. The group has three concepts: the in and not in operators that answer yes or no, the index method that answers with a position, and the short-circuiting of and and or that lets a program ask a question about an item only when the item exists. The chapter teaches in, not in and index, and then short-circuiting (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Searching a list means asking where a value is or whether it is there. The group has three concepts: the in and not in operators that answer yes or no, the index method that answers with a position, and the short-circuiting of and and or that lets a program ask a question about an item only when the item exists. The chapter teaches in, not in and index, and then short-circuiting (Sweigart, 2025).

A list that cannot be searched is only a pile. Almost every program that checks a user's input, looks up a record or avoids a duplicate begins with one of these questions. They also teach, in the order of the group, how Python reports a failed search: in answers with False, and index answers with an error.

The first concept explains in and not in with the pet-name program. The second explains index and its first-match rule, and the third explains how len(spam) > 0 and spam[0] == 'cat' stays safe on an empty list.

nodes.label: In and not in operators
nodes.body: You can determine whether a value is or is not in a list with the in and not in operators. Like other operators they occur in expressions and connect two values: a value to look for and the list where it may be found. The expression evaluates to a Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['hello', 'hi', 'howdy', 'heyas'], 'howdy' in spam is True, 'cat' in spam is False, 'howdy' not in spam is False and 'cat' not in spam is True. The documentation says that x in s is True if an item of s is equal to x, and False otherwise (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: You can determine whether a value is or is not in a list with the in and not in operators. Like other operators they occur in expressions and connect two values: a value to look for and the list where it may be found. The expression evaluates to a Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['hello', 'hi', 'howdy', 'heyas'], 'howdy' in spam is True, 'cat' in spam is False, 'howdy' not in spam is False and 'cat' not in spam is True. The documentation says that x in s is True if an item of s is equal to x, and False otherwise (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A yes or no question about a collection is the commonest test in a program, and the operator reads like the English sentence. It also replaces a loop: without in, a program would walk the list item by item and compare each with the value, and with in the walk is done inside Python. The same operator works on strings, on tuples, on ranges and, in the next chapter, on dictionaries, so it is one of the most widely reused ideas of the course.

The chapter's program myPets.py keeps my_pets = ['Zophie', 'Pooka', 'Fat-tail'], asks for a pet name with input, and prints I do not have a pet named Footfoot when the name is not in the list, and the name followed by is my pet when it is. In the executed run, the entry Footfoot gives exactly the first message. The test is by equality, not by identity: 1 in [1.0] is True because 1 == 1.0. On strings the same operator tests for a substring, so 'ab' in 'cabd' is True although 'ab' in ['cabd'] is False.

Python compares the value with the items from the first to the last, using ==, and stops at the first match. The time it takes therefore grows with the length of the list, and a membership test on a long list that is made again and again in a loop is a known source of slow programs; the data structures of a later chapter answer the question in constant time. The result is always a Boolean, so the operator can be used directly in an if statement.

Keep in mind that the not in operator is distinct from the Boolean not operator (Sweigart, 2025). The expression not x in spam is read as not (x in spam) and gives the same answer as x not in spam, but the second form reads as one test and is the one programmers write. A second slip is to test a list with a value of another type, for example the string '3' against a list of integers, which is simply False and raises no error, so a surprising False should be checked for a type mismatch before the list is doubted.

nodes.definition: The in operator gives True if a value equals an item of the list and False otherwise, and not in gives the opposite.

nodes.label: Index method
nodes.body: List values have an index method that can be passed a value. If that value exists in the list, the method returns the index of the value; if it is not in the list, Python produces a ValueError (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['hello', 'hi', 'howdy', 'heyas'], spam.index('hello') is 0 and spam.index('heyas') is 3. When the list contains duplicates of the value, the method returns the index of its first appearance: for ['Zophie', 'Pooka', 'Fat-tail', 'Pooka'] it returns 1 for 'Pooka' and not 3.

paras.text: List values have an index method that can be passed a value. If that value exists in the list, the method returns the index of the value; if it is not in the list, Python produces a ValueError (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['hello', 'hi', 'howdy', 'heyas'], spam.index('hello') is 0 and spam.index('heyas') is 3. When the list contains duplicates of the value, the method returns the index of its first appearance: for ['Zophie', 'Pooka', 'Fat-tail', 'Pooka'] it returns 1 for 'Pooka' and not 3.

The operator in says that a value is there, and the method index says where. The position is what a program needs in order to replace the item, to delete it with del or to look at its neighbours. The two together make the usual search idiom: ask with in, and only then ask with index, so that the failure case is handled before it can raise an error.

In the executed examples the index of 'hello' is 0, the index of 'heyas' is 3 and the first 'Pooka' is at 1. The method accepts a start and an end as optional arguments, so ['a', 'b', 'a'].index('a', 1) is 2: the search starts at position 1 and finds the second 'a'. Searching for a value that is absent, as with spam.index('howdy howdy howdy'), raises a ValueError. Under Python 3.14 the message is list.index(x): x not in list, whereas Python 3.12 and 3.13, like the printed chapter, give the older wording 'howdy howdy howdy' is not in list.

The method compares the value with the items from the start position onward, using ==, and returns the position of the first one that matches; if it reaches the end it raises the error. Like in, it takes time proportional to the length of the list. It returns a number, so the answer can be used as an index at once, which is the reason the method raises an error rather than returning a special value: a returned -1 would be a valid index that means the last item (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The error is the point of the method and must be planned for. A program that calls index on a value that may be missing should test with in first, or catch the ValueError with try and except, which the later chapter on errors explains. Do not forget the first-match rule: a list with duplicates has several positions for the same value, and index gives only the first. To find all of them, loop with enumerate, which is explained in the branch on loops.

nodes.definition: The index method returns the index of the first item equal to the value and raises a ValueError if there is none.

error.out: ValueError: list.index(x): x not in list

nodes.label: Short-circuiting
nodes.body: Boolean operators have a subtle behaviour that is easy to miss. If either value combined by and is False the whole expression is False, and if either value combined by or is True the whole expression is True. For the expression False and spam it does not matter whether spam is True or False, because the answer is already False; Python uses this fact to skip the right-hand side altogether. This shortcut is called short-circuiting (Sweigart, 2025). The reference states the rule exactly: x and y evaluates x first and, if x is false, returns it, otherwise evaluates y (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Boolean operators have a subtle behaviour that is easy to miss. If either value combined by and is False the whole expression is False, and if either value combined by or is True the whole expression is True. For the expression False and spam it does not matter whether spam is True or False, because the answer is already False; Python uses this fact to skip the right-hand side altogether. This shortcut is called short-circuiting (Sweigart, 2025). The reference states the rule exactly: x and y evaluates x first and, if x is false, returns it, otherwise evaluates y (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Short-circuiting is more than a speed-up, and the chapter shows why on a list. A program that reads the first item of a list that may be empty would fail with an IndexError. Putting the question whether the list has any items on the left of an and makes the right side run only when it is safe. The pattern guard and then use is one of the most common in real programs, and it turns a crash into a quiet False.

The chapter's first version reads spam[0] == 'cat' directly, and for spam = ['cat', 'dog'] it prints A cat is the first item. For the empty list the same line raises an IndexError, and the corrected condition len(spam) > 0 and spam[0] == 'cat' evaluates to False and so prints The first item is not a cat. In the executed examples the guarded condition gives False for [] and True for ['cat', 'dog'], and the expression True or [][0] is True without any error, since or also stops early.

For and, Python evaluates the left operand and, if it is false, returns that operand without looking at the right one; if it is true, the result is the right operand. For or the rule is mirrored: a true left operand is returned and the right is skipped. The operators return one of their operands, not necessarily True or False, so [] and 5 is [] and [] or 5 is 5. The empty list counts as false, as do the empty string and zero, which is why many programmers write if spam: where the chapter writes if len(spam) > 0.

The order of the operands matters, and the guard must come first: spam[0] == 'cat' and len(spam) > 0 still raises the error. A second trap is to put an expression with a side effect, such as a call that changes a list, on the right of and or or and to forget that it may never run. Keep the right operand free of side effects, or use an if statement when the order of actions matters.

nodes.definition: The operators and and or stop as soon as the left operand decides the result and do not evaluate the right operand, so a test on the left can guard an expression on the right.

nodes.label: Ordering a list
nodes.body: Ordering a list means putting its items in a sequence by comparison: numbers from small to large, strings from first to last in the dictionary. The group has four concepts: the sort method, its key and reverse arguments, the reverse method, and the function sorted that gives a new ordered list. The chapter teaches sort and reverse (Sweigart, 2025), and the documentation adds the function sorted (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Ordering a list means putting its items in a sequence by comparison: numbers from small to large, strings from first to last in the dictionary. The group has four concepts: the sort method, its key and reverse arguments, the reverse method, and the function sorted that gives a new ordered list. The chapter teaches sort and reverse (Sweigart, 2025), and the documentation adds the function sorted (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Sorted data is easier for people to read and for programs to search, to merge and to compare. The group also brings the first clear case in the course of a design choice that runs through Python: a method that changes a list in place returns None, while a function that makes a new list returns it.

The first concept explains sort and its three cautions: it works in place, it cannot compare numbers with strings, and it orders strings by their character codes. The second explains key and reverse, the third reverse, and the fourth sorted.

nodes.label: Sort method
nodes.body: You can sort lists of number values or lists of strings with the sort method. It returns the numbers in numerical order and the strings in alphabetical order; with spam holding [2, 5, 3.14, 1, -7], the call spam.sort() leaves [-7, 1, 2, 3.14, 5], and with ['Ants', 'Cats', 'Dogs', 'Badgers', 'Elephants'] it leaves ['Ants', 'Badgers', 'Cats', 'Dogs', 'Elephants'] (Sweigart, 2025). The documentation adds that the method modifies the sequence in place for economy of space when sorting a large sequence, and that it returns None to remind the reader that it works by side effect (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

It returns the numbers in numerical order and the strings in alphabetical order; with spam holding [2, 5, 3.14, 1, -7], the call spam.sort() leaves [-7, 1, 2, 3.14, 5], and with ['Ants', 'Cats', 'Dogs', 'Badgers', 'Elephants'] it leaves ['Ants', 'Badgers', 'Cats', 'Dogs', 'Elephants'] (Sweigart, 2025). The documentation adds that the method modifies the sequence in place for economy of space when sorting a large sequence, and that it returns None to remind the reader that it works by side effect (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The chapter lists three things to note about sort, and each of them is a lesson about the language. The method works in place, so it teaches the difference between changing a list and making one. It needs items that can be compared, so it teaches that Python does not guess. And it orders strings by character code, so it teaches that a computer's idea of alphabetical order is not a person's. A student who understands these three points will not be surprised by most sorting problems.

In the executed examples, spam = spam.sort() leaves spam equal to None, because sort returns None after it has sorted the old list, and the sorted list is lost. A list that mixes numbers and strings, [1, 3, 2, 4, 'Alice', 'Bob'], raises a TypeError, because Python does not know how to compare them; the message is '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'. Strings are ordered by character code, so ['Alice', 'ants', 'Bob', 'badgers', 'Carol', 'cats'] becomes ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'ants', 'badgers', 'cats'], with every capital letter before every lower-case letter.

The method uses the algorithm called Timsort, which finds runs of items that are already ordered and merges them, and which the documentation describes as stable: items that compare equal keep their original order (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Python compares two items with the less-than operator, so any items that support it can be sorted, which is why numbers and strings work and why a number and a string do not. The comparison of strings goes character by character by code point, and the code of Z is lower than that of a.

Never write spam = spam.sort(): the list is sorted, then the name is rebound to the None that the method returned, and the data is lost. If a sorted copy is wanted and the original must stay as it is, use the function sorted, described below. If the order of strings must ignore the case, pass key=str.lower, which the next concept explains.

nodes.definition: The sort method orders the items of the list in place, from small to large, and returns None; it cannot compare numbers with strings and orders strings by character code.

error.out: TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'

nodes.label: Key and reverse arguments
nodes.body: The sort method takes two keyword-only arguments. Passing True as the reverse argument sorts the values in reverse order: after spam.sort() the call spam.sort(reverse=True) leaves ['Elephants', 'Dogs', 'Cats', 'Badgers', 'Ants'] (Sweigart, 2025). If the values should be sorted in regular alphabetical order, the chapter passes str.lower as the key argument, so ['a', 'z', 'A', 'Z'] becomes ['a', 'A', 'z', 'Z']. This argument causes sort to treat all the items in the list as if they were lowercase without actually changing the values in the list.
