nodes.label: Matrix screensaver
nodes.body: In the science fiction film The Matrix, computer monitors display streams of glowing green numbers, like digital rain pouring down a glass window. The chapter's screensaver imitates it with a list: the list columns holds 70 integers, one for each column of output, and the number of columns is the constant WIDTH (Sweigart, 2025). When an integer in columns is 0, the program prints an empty space for that column; when it is greater than 0, it prints a random 1 or 0 and counts the integer down.

paras.text: In the science fiction film The Matrix, computer monitors display streams of glowing green numbers, like digital rain pouring down a glass window. The chapter's screensaver imitates it with a list: the list columns holds 70 integers, one for each column of output, and the number of columns is the constant WIDTH (Sweigart, 2025). When an integer in columns is 0, the program prints an empty space for that column; when it is greater than 0, it prints a random 1 or 0 and counts the integer down.

The program shows the list as a set of counters, a use that is quite different from a list of names. The list's length is fixed by the width of the window and only its values change, so the design is simple: each column is independent and the whole screen is the list read from left to right. The constant WIDTH has an all-uppercase name by convention, so that columns = [0] * WIDTH explains itself better than columns = [0] * 70 (van Rossum, Warsaw and Coghlan, 2001).

The infinite loop prints one row per pass. For each column, there is a two percent chance, tested by random.random() < 0.02, that the integer is set to a random number between 4 and 14; random.randint(4, 14) gives it. Then the column prints a space if its counter is 0, and otherwise a random choice from [0, 1] and decrements the counter. A pause of a tenth of a second between rows, time.sleep(0.1), and the handling of KeyboardInterrupt by an except block that calls sys.exit() end the program. In the executed run of 200 rows every row has exactly 70 characters, only spaces, 0 and 1 appear, and some rows are not blank.

Python builds the list by replicating [0] seventy times, which is safe because the items are integers and cannot be changed through a shared reference. The loop for i in range(WIDTH) visits the indexes of the columns, and columns[i] -= 1 is an augmented assignment on an item. Each stream starts at a random column, runs for 4 to 14 rows and stops by itself when its counter reaches 0, which is the whole animation.

The program runs for ever until the user presses Ctrl-C, so never run it in a test without a bound. Changing WIDTH to more characters than the window is wide makes the lines wrap and spoils the picture. And the constant is only a convention: nothing in Python prevents the program from changing WIDTH later, so the programmer must not.

nodes.definition: The program keeps one counter per output column in a list of WIDTH zeros: a counter above zero means that a stream of binary digits is running in that column and counts the digits left to print.

nodes.label: Comma Code
nodes.body: The first practice program of the chapter asks for a function that takes a list value as an argument and returns a string with all the items separated by a comma and a space, with and inserted before the last item. For the list ['apples', 'bananas', 'tofu', 'cats'] the function returns 'apples, bananas, tofu, and cats'. The function should work with any list passed to it, and the chapter asks the reader to test the case where an empty list is passed (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The first practice program of the chapter asks for a function that takes a list value as an argument and returns a string with all the items separated by a comma and a space, with and inserted before the last item. For the list ['apples', 'bananas', 'tofu', 'cats'] the function returns 'apples, bananas, tofu, and cats'. The function should work with any list passed to it, and the chapter asks the reader to test the case where an empty list is passed (Sweigart, 2025).

The task is small and it contains the whole skill of the chapter: slices for the first items and the last, len for the special cases, and a decision about the empty list. Writing it makes a student face the edge cases that every real function has, and the answer shows how much a slice shortens a loop.

A solution joins all items except the last with ', ', and then adds ', and ' and the last item. In the executed examples the function returns 'apples, bananas, tofu, and cats' for the four-item list, 'apples' for a one-item list and '' for the empty list. For two items the same rule gives 'apples, and bananas'; the chapter does not say how a list of two should read, so the program states its own rule and the course asks the reader to decide whether the comma before and is wanted.

The function tests len(items): zero gives an empty string, one gives the item itself, and any other length takes the slice items[:-1] for the first items, joins them with ', ' and appends ', and ' and items[-1]. The slice items[:-1] is a new list, so the argument is not changed, which matters because of the rule that a function receives the caller's list.

The empty list is the case that the chapter asks to test, because items[-1] on it raises an IndexError. The one-item list is the second edge, where the rule would otherwise produce a lone ', and '. Check also that the function does not change its argument, by comparing the list before and after the call.

nodes.definition: The Comma Code function joins the items of any list into one string, separated by commas, with and before the last item, and must work for the empty list and the one-item list.

nodes.label: Coin Flip Streaks
nodes.body: The second practice program is an experiment. If you flip a coin 100 times and write down an H for each heads and a T for each tails, you create a list like T T T T H H H H T T. A human asked to make up 100 random flips will alternate too much, which looks random to people but is not. The program finds out how often a streak of six heads or six tails comes up in a randomly generated list of 100 flips, and it repeats the experiment 10,000 times so that it can estimate the chance (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The second practice program is an experiment. If you flip a coin 100 times and write down an H for each heads and a T for each tails, you create a list like T T T T H H H H T T. A human asked to make up 100 random flips will alternate too much, which looks random to people but is not. The program finds out how often a streak of six heads or six tails comes up in a randomly generated list of 100 flips, and it repeats the experiment 10,000 times so that it can estimate the chance (Sweigart, 2025).

The program is a simulation, a method that the later chapters use for many questions: when the exact answer is hard to work out, run the experiment many times and count. The chapter notes that some knowledge of mathematics could give the exact answer, but programmers are notoriously bad at math. Here the list does two jobs, as the record of one experiment and as the thing searched by slices.

The chapter's hint is to build the list with a loop that appends random.choice(['H', 'T']) 100 times, and to find a streak by slicing some_list[i:i + 6] and comparing it with ['H'] * 6 and ['T'] * 6. The executed program prints that its estimate lies between 78 and 83 percent. The exact answer, computed from a recurrence for the number of sequences of 100 flips that have no streak of six, is about 80.68 percent, so a streak of six in 100 flips is likelier than not by a wide margin.

For each of 10,000 experiments the program builds a list of 100 flips and looks at every window of six: the starting indexes run from 0 to len(flips) - 6, so range(len(flips) - 5), since the last window must still have six items. The first window that matches counts the experiment and the break ends the search. The final estimate is the number of experiments with a streak divided by 100, which converts a count out of 10,000 to a percentage.

Watch the end of the range: using range(len(flips)) would let the slice run past the end and compare shorter lists, which never match, so the last windows would be silently wasted. Count an experiment once, not once for every streak in it, which is what the break does. The estimate varies from run to run, so test it by a range and not by an exact value.

nodes.definition: The Coin Flip Streaks program simulates 10,000 experiments of 100 coin flips and counts those with a streak of six equal results, found by comparing slices of six items with a list of six H or six T.

lecture.title: Chapter 6: Lists
lecture.say: This deck teaches the list, the first container of Python: one value that holds many values in order and can be changed after it is made. Every console and program on the slides was executed under Python 3.14.6, and the deck checks re-ran them on the finished file, so a result shown here is a result Python printed. The full text of every slide is on the course page for chapter 6, and the four true stories on the slides carry their sources.

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route has six parts and ends with programs that the reader can follow line by line. One story is a note that a Dutch computer scientist wrote in 1982 about starting to count at zero, one is the fair shuffle of 1938 and 1964, one is a toy that answers questions from a list of twenty replies, and one is the green rain of a famous film. The part a reader expects to be hardest is names and copies, and it is worth marking now and checking again at the summary slide.

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The chapter is organised around three competency questions, and they are printed on this slide so that the reader can come back to them at the end. The first asks which list operations read, replace, add, remove, find, order and combine items, and which change the list in place. The second asks how names, copies and function arguments decide whether a change is seen elsewhere in a program. The third asks which printed outputs of the book differ in current Python and which modern forms the book leaves out. Each is answered by a range of slides in this deck, which the agenda names, and in full on the course page for chapter 6. As a question to think about, consider which of the three you could already answer from what you know about variables and strings.

lecture.title: One chapter, six branches
lecture.say: A list is a value that contains multiple values in an ordered sequence. The chapter opens with the observation that lists and their cousin the tuple can hold many values, which makes it easier to write programs that handle large amounts of data, and that since lists can contain other lists they can arrange data in hierarchical structures (Sweigart, 2025). The count under each branch is how many concepts the course page explains for it; the deck walks the branches in order, and the fifth, names and copies, is the one that surprises most beginners. As a question to think about, consider why a chapter about a container needs a whole branch about names. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Sequences and references and The list data type, in the concepts The list data type, Sequences and references.

lecture.title: The list as a value
lecture.say: A list value is the list itself, as opposed to the values inside it. The chapter makes the distinction in its first sentences: the term list value refers to the list, which can be stored in a variable or passed to a function like any other value, and not to the values inside the list value (Sweigart, 2025). The picture is the book's own figure of a list and the four indexes that reach its items, which the next slides try out in a console. As a question to think about, consider what a row of four lockers would have to look like for the first one to be number zero. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under List values and Positions in a list, in the concepts List values, Positions in a list.

lecture.title: Indexes: a row of numbered lockers
lecture.say: An index is the integer inside the square brackets that follow a list, and it names the position of the item to select. With spam holding ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant'], spam[0] evaluates to 'cat', spam[1] to 'bat', and so on. Read the console from the top: the first four rows reach the same list from both ends, the fifth gives the length, and the last row is the error that an index past the end raises. As a question to think about, consider what spam[len(spam)] would give, and why the largest valid index is one less than the length. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Positions in a list, in the concepts Index, Negative index.

lecture.title: Why the first item is number zero
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 1982-08-11. On 11 August 1982 Edsger Dijkstra, at home in Nuenen, wrote a short note called 'Why numbering should start at zero'. He asked how to write the numbers 2 to 12 without three dots, compared four ways of writing the bounds, and chose 2 <= i < 13: the difference of the bounds is the length, and two neighbouring ranges meet without a gap. For a sequence of N items the same choice gives 0 <= i < N, so an element's number equals the count of elements before it. The note was triggered by a mathematician who called young computing scientists pedantic for counting from zero. Python's spam[0] and spam[1:3] follow this convention. The console cuts items 2 to 5 out of a list of ten, finds that the slice has 5 minus 2 items, and shows that two neighbouring slices put together make the whole list again. The lesson of the story, in one sentence, is this. Counting from zero makes the index equal to the number of items before it. The sources are these. E. W. Dijkstra, 'Why numbering should start at zero', EWD831, Nuenen, 11 August 1982 (transcription at cs.utexas.edu/~EWD/transcriptions/EWD08xx/EWD831.html). Photo: Edsger Dijkstra, 1994, by Andreas F. Borchert, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

lecture.title: Slices: a part of a list, as a new list
lecture.say: A slice gets several values from a list in the form of a new list. It is entered between square brackets, like an index, but with two integers separated by a colon. Each row of the console cuts the same four-item list differently, and the last row applies a step of three to the numbers 0 to 9, which keeps 0, 3, 6 and 9. As a question to think about, consider how many items spam[1:3] holds, and how you could have known without running it. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Slicing, in the concepts Slice, Omitted slice ends, Slice step.

lecture.title: Replace, add, remove
lecture.say: Item assignment puts a variable name on the left of an assignment statement normally, as in spam = 42, but a list index can stand there instead: the assignment changes the value at that index (Sweigart, 2025). With spam holding ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant'], the statement spam[1] = 'aardvark' means that the value at index 1 in the list spam is assigned the string 'aardvark', and the list becomes ['cat', 'aardvark', 'rat', 'elephant']. After each change the console shows the list or the value returned, so the order of the rows is the order in which the list changes. As a question to think about, consider which of the three ways to remove an item you would use when you know its position and which when you know its value. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Adding items and Removing items and Replacing items, in the concepts Item assignment, append, insert, pop, remove.

lecture.title: Combine and search
lecture.say: List concatenation joins two lists end to end with the plus operator. The expression [1, 2, 3] + ['A', 'B', 'C'] evaluates to [1, 2, 3, 'A', 'B', 'C']. On the left the plus sign gives a new list while extend changes the old one; on the right in answers True or False and index answers with a place, or with an error when the value is absent. As a question to think about, consider why an expression that begins with an empty list and the word and never reaches the index that would fail. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Combining lists and Searching a list, in the concepts List concatenation, in and not in operators, index method.

lecture.title: Order a list
lecture.say: You can sort lists of number values or lists of strings with the sort method. It returns the numbers in numerical order and the strings in alphabetical order; with spam holding [2, 5, 3.14, 1, -7], the call spam.sort() leaves [-7, 1, 2, 3.14, 5], and with ['Ants', 'Cats', 'Dogs', 'Badgers', 'Elephants'] it leaves ['Ants', 'Badgers', 'Cats', 'Dogs', 'Elephants'] (Sweigart, 2025). The first rows sort the numbers in place and then backwards, the next two rows show that plain sorting puts every capital letter before every small one and that the key argument repairs this, and the last row is the TypeError of a list that mixes a number and a word. As a question to think about, consider when you would choose sorted over sort. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Ordering a list, in the concepts sort method, key and reverse arguments, sorted function.

lecture.title: Twenty answers in a toy, nine in the program
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 1946 (patent filed), 1950 (the eight-ball shape). The Magic 8 Ball was invented in 1946 by Albert Carter and Abe Bookman, whose company Alabe Crafts in Cincinnati first sold it as a cylinder, and in 1950 made it the black-and-white eight ball we know. Inside, a twenty-sided die floats in dark blue liquid, and each face carries one answer: ten affirmative, five neutral and five negative. The chapter's program keeps nine of those answers, such as 'It is certain' and 'Very doubtful', in a Python list and prints one at a random index. A tenth answer needs no new code, which is the point of the list. On the slide, the program prints three of the nine answers at random indexes, with the random seed fixed so that every run shows the same three answers. The lesson of the story, in one sentence, is this. Put the answers in a list and the program need not change. The sources are these. Magic 8 Ball, Wikipedia (history, the 20 answers and their split); the answer list of the program in Sweigart (2025), chapter 6. Photo: the answer 'It is certain.' on a Magic 8 Ball, by Zaneology, Dallas, 2012, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

lecture.title: Loops and unpacking
lecture.say: Technically, a for loop repeats its block once for each item in a list value (Sweigart, 2025). The group explains the four forms that matter in practice: the loop over the indexes, the loop that counts with enumerate, the loop that must not change its own list, and the comprehension that replaces a loop that builds a list. The picture is the book's figure of a list whose items each carry a numbered tag, which is what enumerate pairs with the items. As a question to think about, consider when you need the position of an item and when the item alone is enough. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Looping over a list and Unpacking a list, in the concepts Looping over a list, Unpacking a list.

lecture.title: Loop over a list
lecture.say: Instead of the range(len(some_list)) technique, a program can call the enumerate function. On each iteration of the loop, enumerate returns two values: the index of the item in the list, and the item in the list itself (Sweigart, 2025). The bars are computed, not typed: the second console row is the list of lengths [4, 8, 13, 7] that gives their heights, and the first row shows the pairs that enumerate produces. As a question to think about, consider why enumerate is usually clearer than a loop over range(len(supplies)). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Looping over a list, in the concepts enumerate function, Loop over the indexes, List comprehension.

lecture.title: Never remove from the list you loop over
lecture.say: Code that changes a list while a for loop is walking through that same list can be tricky to get right, as the tutorial warns, and the usual advice is to loop over a copy of the collection or to create a new collection (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The behaviour has a simple cause: the loop does not remember the items, it remembers a position, and it asks the list for the item at that position on every pass. The loop meant to remove all four letters removes only two and leaves b and d, because each removal moves the next item into the place the loop has just passed; the bars below the console show what a comprehension builds without touching the source. As a question to think about, consider what the loop would have left if the list had held six letters. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Looping over a list, in the concepts Changing a list during a loop, List comprehension.

lecture.title: Unpacking: names for the items
lecture.say: The multiple assignment trick, technically called tuple unpacking, is a shortcut that lets you assign multiple variables with the values in a list in one line of code (Sweigart, 2025). Instead of writing size = cat[0], color = cat[1] and disposition = cat[2], the program writes size, color, disposition = cat, with cat holding ['fat', 'gray', 'loud']. The first two rows give three names to three items; the starred row gives first one item and rest the other three; the swap exchanges two values; and the last row is the ValueError of a count that does not match. As a question to think about, consider how many items a starred name receives when the list has exactly as many items as the other names. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Unpacking a list, in the concepts Multiple assignment trick, Starred unpacking.

lecture.title: Names and copies
lecture.say: A common metaphor is that variables are boxes that store values, but this explanation is a simplification of what Python does. A better metaphor is that variables are paper name tags attached to values with string (Sweigart, 2025). The picture is the book's figure of a number with a name tag and then two tags, which shows that assignment attaches a tag to a value and does not copy the value. As a question to think about, consider what the third panel of the picture says happens to the old value when spam receives a new one. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Names and references and Sequence types, in the concepts Names and references, Sequence types.

lecture.title: Two names, one list
lecture.say: When you assign 42 to the variable spam, you are creating the 42 value in the computer's memory and storing a reference to it in the variable. When you copy the value in spam and assign it to eggs, you are copying the reference; both variables refer to the same 42 (Sweigart, 2025). After eggs receives the new item spam shows it too and the is operator confirms that both names point at one list; the last four rows show that a function which appends to its parameter changes the list the caller passed. As a question to think about, consider what a program must do when it needs to change a list without the caller seeing the change. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Names and references, in the concepts Aliasing, Lists as function arguments.

lecture.title: Copies: shallow and deep
lecture.say: The function copy.copy can make a duplicate copy of a mutable value like a list. After import copy, spam = ['A', 'B', 'C'] and cheese = copy.copy(spam), the assignment cheese[1] = 42 changes the copy and leaves spam as ['A', 'B', 'C'], while cheese becomes ['A', 42, 'C']. After the first change the shallow copy shows 99 in the inner list it shares with the original, while the deep copy still shows 1; the last three rows show that two rows made by repetition change together. As a question to think about, consider how you would build a grid of three rows of three zeros that does not share its rows. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Copying lists and Names and references, in the concepts Shallow copy, Deep copy, Repeating a list of lists.

lecture.title: A fair shuffle with a pencil, then with a computer
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 1938 (pencil and paper), 1964 (computer version). In 1938 Ronald Fisher and Frank Yates printed a pencil-and-paper way to put numbers into random order in their book of statistical tables. In 1964 Richard Durstenfeld published a computer version in the Communications of the ACM, which swaps each item with a randomly chosen one that is not behind it, and Donald Knuth described it in his series on algorithms. The method gives every order the same chance. It is what Python's random.shuffle still does: its source walks the list from the end and swaps each place with a random place at or before it. The console deals three cards six thousand times, counts how often each of the six possible orders appears and subtracts the expected one thousand; the largest difference is 45 deals in six thousand, which is what a fair shuffle gives, and the bars show the six differences. The lesson of the story, in one sentence, is this. A shuffle is only fair if every order is equally likely. The sources are these. R. A. Fisher and F. Yates, Statistical Tables for Biological, Agricultural and Medical Research (Oliver and Boyd, 1938); R. Durstenfeld, 'Algorithm 235: Random permutation', Communications of the ACM 7(7), 1964, p. 420; D. E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 2 (Algorithm P); CPython's Lib/random.py. Photo: Ronald Aylmer Fisher, 1952, by Barry Eagel, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

lecture.title: The green rain that was never a code
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 1999 (film), 2017 (the designer's remark). The falling green characters of the film The Matrix (1999) come from a typeface that Simon Whiteley designed: mirrored half-width Japanese kana, Latin letters and numerals. In a 2017 CNET interview he joked that the code was made from the sushi recipes of his wife's cookbooks, a story that others have since questioned. The chapter's screensaver imitates the rain with a list of 70 counters, one per column: a counter above zero prints a random 0 or 1 and counts down, and a counter at zero prints a space. The effect is a whole animation made from one list. The program keeps one counter per column in a list: a counter above zero prints a random digit and counts down, and a counter at zero prints a space, so streams of digits start and end on their own. The lesson of the story, in one sentence, is this. A list of counters can animate a screen. The sources are these. Matrix digital rain, Wikipedia (designer, glyphs, the 2017 CNET interview); the screensaver program in Sweigart (2025), chapter 6. Image: Figure 6-5 of Sweigart (2025), the chapter's own screensaver running in a console window, CC BY-NC-SA.

lecture.title: Comma Code: a list into a sentence
lecture.say: The first practice program of the chapter asks for a function that takes a list value as an argument and returns a string with all the items separated by a comma and a space, with and inserted before the last item. For the list ['apples', 'bananas', 'tofu', 'cats'] the function returns 'apples, bananas, tofu, and cats'. The function joins everything but the last item with commas and then adds the word and and the last item; the four transcripts show the usual case, the two-item case, the one-item case and the empty list. As a question to think about, consider which of the four test lists would fail if the function always put a comma before the and. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Programs with lists and Slicing, in the concepts Comma Code, Slice.

lecture.title: Coin Flip Streaks: a simulation with lists
lecture.say: The second practice program is an experiment. If you flip a coin 100 times and write down an H for each heads and a T for each tails, you create a list like T T T T H H H H T T. Each pass of the outer loop makes one list of a hundred flips and the inner loop walks along it, extending the current run when two neighbours are equal and restarting it otherwise; the single line printed is the percentage of experiments whose longest run reached six. As a question to think about, consider why the fixed random seed matters if you want to compare two versions of the program. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 6, under Programs with lists and Random selection and ordering, in the concepts Coin Flip Streaks, random.choice.

lecture.title: The chapter in five lines
lecture.say: These five lines are the deck in miniature, one per part, and each of them is carried by a range of slides that the agenda names. A line that feels unproven should send the reader back to its consoles, because every result in it was executed. The full text behind all five lines is on the course page for chapter 6.

lecture.title: Where to go from here
lecture.say: Everything here is free to read, and every link was opened on the date in the subtitle. A good exercise is to paste the aliasing console of this deck into Python Tutor and watch the two name tags arrive on one list, and then to read the official sorting guide for the key argument. The course page for chapter 6 carries the full resource list with a sentence on why each entry is there.

lecture.title: What you should now be able to say
lecture.say: Four claims, each carried by consoles and programs that ran on a slide of this deck. The course page for chapter 6 carries every word behind them, the four stories with their sources, and the question bank to test the four claims on yourself.

ndiag.title: How a program asks whether a value is in a list and where
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, the Searching a list group: in and not in (an expression that evaluates to True or False), index (returns the position of the first match, raises a ValueError when the value is absent), and short-circuiting (a test on the left of and guards an expression on the right)
ndiag.why: the explanations describe what the programmer does in order - ask whether the value is in the list, ask for its position only when it is there, guard the item with a test of the length when the list may be empty - with choices on the way: a workflow

nodes.label: Is the value in the list? Test it with the in operator
The expression evaluates to False: the value is not in the list
Is the position of the value needed?
Call the index method: it returns the index of the first match
Does the program read the first item of a list that may be empty?
Write len(spam) > 0 and spam[0] == 'cat': short-circuiting protects
Use the value, which is True for the in operator

ndiag.title: Choosing how to remove an item from a list
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, the Removing items group: del (when you know the index of the value you want to remove), remove (when you know the value itself; the first match only; a ValueError when it is absent), pop (removes the item at an index, by default the last, and returns it; an IndexError on an empty list)
ndiag.why: the passage is a choice made step by step from what the programmer knows - the index or the value - and whether the removed item is needed afterwards, which is a workflow with decisions

nodes.label: Does the programmer know the index of the value to remove?
Is the removed item needed afterwards?
Call the pop method: it removes the item and returns it
Use the del statement: it removes the item at the index
Call the remove method with the value itself
The first match is removed; later matches stay in the list
Is the value missing from the list?
Python raises a ValueError: the value is not in the list

ndiag.title: Choosing the form of a loop over a list
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6 and the Python documentation, the Looping over a list group: a for loop over the items, range(len(...)) for the indexes, enumerate for the index and the item, a list comprehension for a new list, and the warning not to change a list while a loop is walking through it
ndiag.why: the group compares forms by what the loop body needs - the item, the index, both, or a new list - and warns about one case, which is a choice walked through question by question: a workflow

nodes.label: Does the loop build a new list from the old one?
Write a list comprehension: an expression, a for clause and an if clause
Does the loop remove or add items of the list it is reading?
Loop over a copy or build a new list instead of changing the old one
Does the loop body need the index of each item?
Use enumerate: it returns the index and the item on each iteration
Loop over the list itself: the loop variable is each item in turn
Must the loop change items in place by index?
Use range(len(some_list)) to iterate over the indexes

ndiag.title: The life of a list: from empty to filled and back
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, the List and Changing a list sections: the empty list [] contains no values; append, insert and extend add items; del, remove and pop take items away; the length of a list changes as items are added or removed
ndiag.why: the explanations describe the states a list is in - empty, with items - and the events that move it from one to the next, append and its relatives forward and pop and its relatives back: a life cycle

states.label: Empty: the list [] contains no values and its length is 0
Filled: the list holds items in order and has a length
Changed in place: items replaced, added or removed

transitions: append, insert or extend adds items
append, insert or extend adds more items
an item is replaced by assignment to an index
the list is still one list, now with other items
del, remove or pop takes the last item away

ndiag.title: A list and its names: shared, then copied
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, the References and Copying groups: a variable holds a reference; the assignment copies only the reference, so two names refer to one list; copy.copy makes a separate list that shares the inner lists; copy.deepcopy copies the inner lists as well
ndiag.why: the passage follows one list through the states it is in as the program assigns, copies and changes it - one name, shared by two names, copied shallowly, copied deeply - and the events that move it on: a life cycle

states.label: One name: a variable refers to the list
Shared: two names refer to the same list
Shallow copy: a separate list that shares the inner lists
Deep copy: separate lists, nothing shared with the original

transitions: eggs = spam copies only the reference
a change made through either name shows through both
copy.copy makes a duplicate of the list
a change to an inner list shows through both
copy.deepcopy copies the inner lists as well

ndiag.title: What happens when a function receives a list
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, the Arguments passage of the References section: when a function is called, Python copies the reference of the argument to the parameter variable, so for a list the code in the function modifies the original value in place
ndiag.why: the passage is an exchange between the calling code, the function and the list in an order that matters - the call, the copy of the reference, the append, the return, the print - which is an interaction

messages: spam = [1, 2, 3]: the variable refers to the list
eggs(spam): Python copies the reference to the parameter
some_parameter.append('Hello') modifies the list in place
returns: the function gives no new value back

ndiag.title: Copying a list that contains lists: what is shared
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6 and the copy module documentation: a shallow copy constructs a new compound object and inserts references to the objects found in the original; a deep copy inserts copies; repeating a list of lists repeats references to one inner list
ndiag.why: the passage is an exchange between the program, the copy module and the lists in an order that matters - the program asks for a copy, changes the copy, and looks at the original - and the answer differs between the two functions: an interaction

messages: copy.copy(spam): ask for a shallow copy
a new list that holds references to the same inner lists
the original shows the change too: the inner list is shared
copy.deepcopy(spam): ask for a deep copy
copies of the inner lists as well, nothing shared
a change to the duplicate no longer reaches the original

ndiag.title: Who uses a list, and for what
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, the list data type and the searching and ordering branches: the programmer reads items by index, takes slices, replaces, adds, removes, searches and sorts; the interpreter raises errors for a bad index or a missing value; the user types the names the program checks and asks the Magic 8 Ball
ndiag.why: the passage lists what the programmer, the user and the interpreter do with a list - read, slice, change, search, sort, check, answer - which is a set of uses by actors, not a sequence

ndiag.title: Changing a list in place: replace, add, remove and reorder
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, the Changing a list branch and the Ordering group: replacing by assignment to an index; adding with append, insert and extend; removing with del, remove and pop; reordering with sort, reverse and shuffle; the methods change the list in place and return None, while sorted returns a new list
ndiag.why: the branches classify one topic, the ways a list can be changed, by what the operation does to the list and list the choices under each - a topic and its parts, laid out to remember
